kurals.tamil:
தகுதி எனவொன்று நன்றே பகுதியால்
பாற்பட்டு ஒழுகப் பெறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thakudhi enavondru nandre pakudhiyaal
Paarpattu ozhukap perin.
kurals.meaning: The virtue called “fitness” — impartiality — is truly good when a person acts rightly and fairly toward every group of people alike, whether enemies, strangers or friends.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a referee who calls the game the same way whether the player is his best friend, a stranger, or someone he doesn’t like. That fairness to everyone is what this kural calls a truly good quality.
kurals.university: The chapter opens by naming impartiality with the word தகுதி (thakudhi, “fitness, propriety, worthiness”), implying that fairness is not one virtue among many but the very measure of whether a person is fit to be trusted. The key phrase பகுதியால் பாற்பட்டு (“keeping to what is due in each division”) was read by the medieval commentator Parimelazhagar, and after him by modern commentators such as Solomon Pappaiah and Karunanidhi, as the threefold division of people into enemies, strangers (neutrals) and friends; the test of justice is that the same standard applies across all three. Placing this chapter in the Illaraviyal (the householder’s section) signals that Valluvar sees impartiality as an everyday domestic and civic duty, not only a king’s or judge’s duty (royal justice is treated separately in chapter 55, செங்கோன்மை). The idea parallels the classical definition of justice as rendering to each their due, and Aristotle’s observation that justice, unlike the other virtues, is directed essentially toward others.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A person is considered still further advanced when he regards honest well-wishers, affectionate benefactors, the neutral, mediators, the envious, friends and enemies, the pious and the sinners all with an equal mind.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna lists every kind of person, from friends to enemies to neutral bystanders, and says the advanced person treats them all with the same even mind (sama-buddhi).
hinduism.tie_back: Almost the same list the Kural’s commentators give (friends, strangers, enemies), with the same demand: one equal standard for all of them.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close match: both name friend, neutral and enemy categories and require even-handedness. The Gita frames it as yogic equanimity rather than social justice.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin, and are convinced of the law as transgressors.”
christianity.explanation: James warns churches against giving rich visitors the good seats and poor visitors the floor. Favouritism, “respect of persons,” is called outright sin.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts treat favouring one group over another as a moral failure, and even-handed treatment as the real virtue.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match on partiality. James’s context is rich versus poor rather than friend, stranger and enemy.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses in justice, and do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an commands believers to stay just even toward people they hate. Hostility is no excuse for bending fairness.
islam.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s point that fairness must hold even toward enemies, the hardest of the three “divisions.”
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one on the enemy case. The Qur’an adds a God-conscious framing (“nearer to righteousness”).

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah forbids tilting a judgment either way, whether out of pity for the poor or deference to the powerful.
judaism.tie_back: Same principle as the Kural: every category of person gets the same straight standard.
judaism._accuracy_note: Core biblical statement of impartial judgment. Its categories are poor and mighty rather than friend and enemy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by passing arbitrary judgments does a man become just; a wise man is he who investigates both right and wrong. He who does not judge others arbitrarily, but passes judgment impartially according to the truth, that sagacious man is a guardian of law and is called just.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada’s chapter “The Just” says a person earns the title “just” only by judging impartially and according to truth, not by hasty or biased verdicts.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural and the Dhammapada both define the just person by impartiality, not by status.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Direct match on impartial judgment as the mark of the just. Less emphasis on the friend, stranger and enemy triad.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “But they who give straight judgements to strangers and to the men of the land, and go not aside from what is just, their city flourishes, and the people prosper in it”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod tells his brother that Zeus blesses cities whose judges treat foreigners and citizens with the same straight justice.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Hesiod’s “strangers and men of the land” lines up with the Kural’s strangers and one’s own people, both judged the same way.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match on equal justice for insiders and outsiders. Hesiod’s framing is civic prosperity sent by Zeus.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For this same reason justice, alone of the virtues, is thought to be ‘another’s good’, because it is related to our neighbour; for it does what is advantageous to another, either a ruler or a copartner.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle notes that justice is the one virtue that looks outward to others, so it is tested in how we treat people other than ourselves.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats justice as a relational virtue proved by how fairly we deal with every other person.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics V.1 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Conceptual parallel on justice as other-directed. Aristotle does not list the friend, stranger and enemy groups.

kurals.tamil:
செப்பம் உடையவன் ஆக்கஞ் சிதைவின்றி
எச்சத்திற் கேமாப்பு உடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Seppam udaiyavan aakkanj sidhaivindri
Echchaththirku emaappu udaiththu.
kurals.meaning: The prosperity of an upright, impartial person does not crumble away; it lasts and becomes a secure support even for their descendants.
kurals.elementary: Think of a house built on strong, straight foundations. It doesn’t fall down; the grandchildren can still live in it. Wealth earned fairly is like that house, and it keeps protecting the family.
kurals.university: செப்பம் (seppam, “straightness, rectitude”) is used here as a synonym for naduvu nilaimai, and the couplet makes a claim about consequences: the ஆக்கம் (aakkam, “increase, prosperity”) of the just person is சிதைவின்றி (“without disintegration”) and furnishes ஏமாப்பு (emaappu, “security, protection”) to the எச்சம் (echcham, “what remains after one”), which the commentators read as descendants or posterity. The point is intergenerational: unjust gain may be large but brittle, while justly earned wealth is durable. The idea that righteousness is an inheritance for children’s children is widespread, found in Proverbs, the Psalms, the Qur’anic story of the orphans’ buried treasure, and Hesiod’s claim that the truthful man’s “generation” prospers. The word echcham reappears in Kural 114, where its meaning (offspring or legacy) becomes a matter of commentarial debate.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The Supreme Personality of Godhead said: Son of Pṛthā, a transcendentalist engaged in auspicious activities does not meet with destruction either in this world or in the spiritual world; one who does good, My friend, is never overcome by evil.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna reassures Arjuna that a person who does good is never destroyed, in this life or the next.
hinduism.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s promise that right conduct leads to lasting security rather than ruin.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Parallel on the indestructibility of the good person’s gains. The Gita speaks of spiritual progress, not material wealth or descendants.

christianity.quote_or_event: “A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children’s children: and the wealth of the sinner is laid up for the just.”
christianity.explanation: This proverb, part of the Christian Old Testament, says a good person’s legacy reaches even grandchildren, while the wicked person’s wealth ends up with others.
christianity.tie_back: Almost the Kural’s exact claim: the upright person’s wealth lasts and benefits their descendants.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close match: lasting wealth plus benefit to descendants. The text is shared with the Hebrew Bible.

islam.quote_or_event: “And as for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city, and there was beneath it a treasure for them, and their father had been righteous. So your Lord intended that they reach maturity and extract their treasure, as a mercy from your Lord.”
islam.explanation: In the story of Moses and al-Khidr, a wall is repaired so that two orphans’ hidden treasure stays safe, explicitly because their father had been righteous.
islam.tie_back: The righteous father’s goodness protects his children’s wealth after him, which is the Kural’s “security to posterity.”
islam._accuracy_note: Striking narrative parallel of a parent’s righteousness safeguarding the children’s inheritance. The virtue named is general righteousness rather than impartiality specifically.

judaism.quote_or_event: “His seed shall be mighty upon earth: the generation of the upright shall be blessed. Wealth and riches shall be in his house: and his righteousness endureth for ever.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm describes the upright person: their descendants are blessed, their house has wealth, and their righteousness lasts forever.
judaism.tie_back: Same three elements as the Kural: uprightness, lasting prosperity, and blessing to descendants.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one structure. The Psalm grounds it in fear of God rather than impartiality as such.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who acquires his wealth in harmless ways like to a bee that honey gathers, riches mount up for him like ant hill’s rapid growth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells the householder Sigala that wealth gathered without harming anyone grows steadily, the way an anthill rises.
buddhism.tie_back: Both say that wealth gained righteously grows and endures.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on the durability of rightly gained wealth. It does not mention benefit to descendants.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For whoever knows the right and is ready to speak it, far-seeing Zeus gives him prosperity; but whoever deliberately lies in his witness and forswears himself, and so hurts Justice and sins beyond repair, that man’s generation is left obscure thereafter. But the generation of the man who swears truly is better thenceforward.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod says Zeus gives prosperity to the one who speaks what is right, and that this person’s descendants fare better, while the perjurer’s line fades into obscurity.
greek_mythology.tie_back: An exact counterpart: justice brings prosperity that carries over to one’s descendants (echcham).
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Remarkably close: justice leads to prosperity and a better lot for descendants. Hesiod frames it through Zeus and oath-keeping.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Then this must be our notion of the just man, that even when he is in poverty or sickness, or any other seeming misfortune, all things will in the end work together for good to him in life and death”
philosophy.explanation: At the end of the Republic, Socrates concludes that the just person is ultimately secure: whatever happens, things work out for his good.
philosophy.tie_back: Shares the Kural’s conviction that justice yields lasting security rather than eventual collapse.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Agrees on the long-run security of the just. Plato speaks of the soul’s good, not material wealth for descendants.

kurals.tamil:
நன்றே தரினும் நடுவிகந்தாம் ஆக்கத்தை
அன்றே யொழிய விடல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nandre tharinum naduvikandhaam aakkaththai
Andre yozhiya vidal.
kurals.meaning: Even if it seems to bring only good, any gain that comes from abandoning fairness should be let go that very day.
kurals.elementary: Suppose you find out you won a prize only because the judge was your uncle and cheated for you. Even though the prize is nice, the right thing is to give it back right away.
kurals.university: The couplet anticipates the objection that injustice might sometimes pay: நன்றே தரினும் (“even if it yields only good”). Valluvar’s answer is categorical. Gain acquired by நடு இகந்து (“transgressing the middle/the just mean”) must be relinquished அன்றே (“that very day”), with no waiting to see whether it turns out well. The emphasis on immediacy suggests a psychological insight: ill-gotten advantage becomes harder to renounce the longer one holds it. The ethic parallels Socrates’ insistence in the Apology that wealth pursued at the cost of the soul is shameful, the Qur’anic ban on consuming others’ property unjustly, and Hesiod’s warning that seized wealth stays only “for a little time.” Philosophically it is a deontological stance: the injustice of the means cannot be redeemed by the goodness of the outcome.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Bound by a network of hundreds of thousands of desires and absorbed in lust and anger, they secure money by illegal means for sense gratification.”
hinduism.explanation: In describing the “demoniac” nature, Krishna names gathering wealth by unjust means (anyāyena, literally “by non-justice”) as a defining mark.
hinduism.tie_back: The Gita condemns exactly what the Kural tells us to drop: wealth gathered by departing from justice.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Clear condemnation of unjust gain. It does not state the Kural’s positive command to renounce such gain immediately.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus asks what any gain is worth if it costs a person their soul.
christianity.tie_back: Both say that no gain, however great or “good,” is worth the moral loss involved in getting it wrongly.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the logic of weighing gain against inner loss. Jesus is speaking of discipleship rather than impartiality specifically.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not consume one another’s wealth unjustly or send it [in bribery] to the rulers in order that [they might aid] you [to] consume a portion of the wealth of the people in sin, while you know [it is unlawful].”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an forbids taking others’ wealth unjustly, including bribing judges to rule in one’s favour.
islam.tie_back: Gain won by corrupting fair judgment is exactly the “gain beyond the middle” the Kural says to reject.
islam._accuracy_note: Very strong, since bribery is the classic breach of impartiality. It is framed as a prohibition rather than as renouncing gain already held.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is a little with righteousness than great revenues without right.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb says a small income gained justly is worth more than a large one gained unjustly.
judaism.tie_back: Same trade-off as the Kural: prefer less with justice over more without it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near-direct parallel. The Kural adds the urgency of giving it up “that very day.”

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He is indeed virtuous, wise, and righteous who neither for his own sake nor for the sake of another (does any wrong), who does not crave for sons, wealth, or kingdom, and does not desire success by unjust means.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada defines the righteous person as one who does not seek success by unjust means, whether for himself or for others.
buddhism.tie_back: Both refuse success that comes through injustice, however attractive it looks.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match on rejecting unjust success. The Dhammapada is phrased as a character description, not an instruction.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Wealth should not be seized: god-given wealth is much better; for if a man take great wealth violently and perforce, or if he steal it through his tongue, as often happens when gain deceives men’s sense and dishonour tramples down honour, the gods soon blot him out and make that man’s house low, and wealth attends him only for a little time.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod warns that wrongly seized wealth, “when gain deceives men’s sense,” is soon destroyed by the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The phrase “gain deceives men’s sense” matches the Kural’s “even if it seems to give good”: the benefit is an illusion that will not last.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match, including the deceptive appeal of unjust gain. Hesiod stresses divine punishment rather than voluntary renunciation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “are you not ashamed of heaping up the greatest amount of money and honour and reputation, and caring so little about wisdom and truth and the greatest improvement of the soul, which you never regard or heed at all?”
philosophy.explanation: At his trial Socrates says his mission is to shame Athenians who pile up money and reputation while neglecting their souls.
philosophy.tie_back: Both put the integrity of the self above material gain.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares the priority of virtue over gain. Socrates targets greed in general rather than injustice-derived gain specifically.

kurals.tamil:
தக்கார் தகவிலர் என்பது அவரவர்
எச்சத்தாற் காணப்ப படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thakkaar thakavilar enbadhu avaravar
Echchaththaar kaanappa padum.
kurals.meaning: Whether a person was just or unjust is revealed by what they leave behind: the good name or ill fame (or, in the older reading, the children) that outlives them.
kurals.elementary: You can tell what kind of gardener someone was by what is still growing in the garden after they leave. People are like that too: what remains after them shows whether they were fair.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on எச்சம் (echcham, “that which remains”). Parimelazhagar reads it as offspring: the worth of the just is visible in good descendants, a reading reflected in G. U. Pope’s translation (“By each one’s offspring shall the truth be clear”). Mu. Varadarasanar and Karunanidhi instead read it as the reputation, praise or blame, that remains after death, while Solomon Pappaiah combines wealth, fame and the conduct of one’s children. Either way the claim is that a verdict on a life’s justice can only be given in retrospect, from its durable effects. This echoes Solon’s advice to Croesus (in Herodotus) to call no one happy until their end is seen, Jesus’ “by their fruits ye shall know them,” and the hadith that a righteous child is among the deeds that continue after death. Note on the text: all three consulted editions (thirukkural.net, ytamizh.com, Project Madurai) print காணப்ப படும்; many printed editions give காணப் படும். The meaning is unaffected.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “People will always speak of your infamy, and for a respectable person, dishonor is worse than death.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns Arjuna that people’s lasting verdict on his conduct will outlive him, and that a dishonoured name is worse than death.
hinduism.tie_back: Both treat the reputation that survives a person as the real verdict on their character.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Parallel on posthumous reputation as a verdict. The Gita’s context is martial duty, not impartiality.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that true character shows itself in results, the way a tree is known by its fruit.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural likewise says the just and unjust are known by what they produce and leave behind.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong structural match (judge by outcomes). “Fruits” in Matthew means deeds during life rather than legacy after death.

islam.quote_or_event: “When a man dies, his acts come to an end, but three, recurring charity, or knowledge (by which people) benefit, or a pious child, who prays for him (for the deceased).”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that after death only three things keep adding to a person’s account, one of which is a righteous child.
islam.tie_back: Fits both readings of echcham: the good that remains after a person, and especially good offspring.
islam._accuracy_note: Close fit to Parimelazhagar’s “offspring” reading. The hadith concerns ongoing reward rather than revealing worth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The memory of the just is blessed: but the name of the wicked shall rot.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb contrasts the lasting, blessed memory of the just with the decaying name of the wicked.
judaism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Varadarasanar reading: praise or blame after death shows who was just.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one with the “legacy/reputation” interpretation of echcham.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not the sweet smell of flowers, not even the fragrance of sandal, tagara, or jasmine blows against the wind. But the fragrance of the virtuous blows against the wind. Truly the virtuous man pervades all directions with the fragrance of his virtue.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the reputation of virtue spreads everywhere and lasts in a way no perfume can.
buddhism.tie_back: Both see virtue as leaving a lasting, perceptible trace by which the person is known.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Parallel on virtue’s lasting renown. It does not concern judging a person after death or offspring.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “The fame, therefore, of her virtue shall never die, and the immortals shall compose a song that shall be welcome to all mankind in honour of the constancy of Penelope.”
greek_mythology.explanation: In the underworld, Agamemnon’s ghost contrasts Penelope’s undying good name with the hateful song that will follow his murderous wife Clytemnestra.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shows the Kural’s contrast in mythic form: the worthy and the unworthy are told apart by the fame or infamy that outlives them.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good match on enduring fame versus infamy. The virtue praised is fidelity rather than impartiality.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Call him, however, until he die, not happy but fortunate.” … “But in every matter it behoves us to mark well the end”
philosophy.explanation: Solon tells King Croesus that no life can be judged until its end is seen.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it holds that a person’s true worth is visible only from what the whole life finally amounts to.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Parallel on retrospective judgment. Solon judges happiness rather than justice.

kurals.tamil:
கேடும் பெருக்கமும் இல்லல்ல நெஞ்சத்துக்
கோடாமை சான்றோர்க் கணி.
kurals.transliteration:
Kedum perukkamum illalla nenjaththuk
Kodaamai saandrork kani.
kurals.meaning: Loss and gain are bound to come in every life; the ornament of the truly noble is a heart that does not bend away from fairness in either.
kurals.elementary: Some days you win, some days you lose; that happens to everyone. A good person plays fair on both kinds of days, and that fairness is their best jewel.
kurals.university: The first line states a plain fact: கேடும் பெருக்கமும் இல்லல்ல (“ruin and increase are not things that do not exist”), that is, they are inevitable. Parimelazhagar attributes them to past deeds (ūḻ), which is reflected in Pope’s “not mere accident” and Solomon Pappaiah’s “already ordained.” Given that fortune is outside our control, the only thing that distinguishes the சான்றோர் (saandror, “the accomplished/noble”) is நெஞ்சத்துக் கோடாமை, “not bending in the heart.” The verb கோடு (“to bend, to be crooked”) is the key image of the chapter and returns in Kurals 118 and 119. The ethic is close to Stoic doctrine, which separates externals from the governing faculty, and to the Gita’s samatva (evenness in gain and loss). The refrain கோடாமை சான்றோர்க்கு அணி is repeated word for word in Kural 118.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Do thou fight for the sake of fighting, without considering happiness or distress, loss or gain, victory or defeat – and by so doing you shall never incur sin.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna to treat gain and loss, victory and defeat as equal and keep doing his duty.
hinduism.tie_back: Matches the Kural’s lābha-alābha (gain and loss) theme: stay steady in right action whatever fortune brings.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close match on equanimity amid gain and loss. The Gita’s application is duty in battle rather than fairness to others.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound”
christianity.explanation: Paul writes from prison that he has learned to stay the same person in poverty and plenty.
christianity.tie_back: Both portray inner steadiness through ups and downs as the mark of a mature person.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good parallel on steadiness in fortune and misfortune. Paul speaks of contentment rather than fairness.

islam.quote_or_event: “In order that you not despair over what has eluded you and not exult [in pride] over what He has given you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an explains that knowing all events are decreed should keep believers from both despair at loss and arrogance at gain.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural (as Parimelazhagar reads it), it accepts loss and gain as ordained and asks for an unshaken heart in both.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match, including the idea that fortunes are ordained. The Qur’an does not tie this to impartiality.

judaism.quote_or_event: “till I die I will not remove mine integrity from me. My righteousness I hold fast, and will not let it go: my heart shall not reproach me so long as I live.”
judaism.explanation: Job, having lost wealth, children and health, refuses to give up his integrity.
judaism.tie_back: Job is the model of a heart that does not bend when ruin comes, the Kural’s kōdāmai.
judaism._accuracy_note: Powerful match on integrity through loss. Job’s integrity is broader than impartiality.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so the wise are not affected by praise or blame.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares the wise to a rock that storms cannot move. The next verse adds that they show no elation or depression in happiness or sorrow.
buddhism.tie_back: The same picture of the noble person’s steady heart amid the “worldly winds” of gain and loss.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match on unshakable equanimity. Praise and blame stand in for the Kural’s loss and gain.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus, back in his own house disguised as a beggar and seeing the suitors’ outrages, restrains his rising heart by reminding it that it has endured worse before, and keeps to his course rather than acting rashly.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus is the Greek model of a man who stays steady through twenty years of loss and reversal.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Shares the ideal of a heart that does not swerve under changing fortune, though Odysseus’ steadiness is about endurance, not fairness.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Weak-to-moderate: endurance rather than impartiality.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Don’t demand that things happen as you wish, but wish that they happen as they do happen, and you will go on well.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus teaches that outcomes are not in our control, and that serenity comes from accepting them while governing our own choices.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s structure is the same: fortune is not ours to command; the uprightness of the heart is.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel with Stoic ethics. Epictetus stresses acceptance more than fairness.

kurals.tamil:
கெடுவல்யான் என்பது அறிகதன் நெஞ்சம்
நடுவொரீஇ அல்ல செயின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Keduval yaan enbadhu arika than nenjam
Naduvoreei alla seyin.
kurals.meaning: If a person’s heart leaves fairness and turns to wrongdoing, let them recognize it as a sure sign: “I am heading for ruin.”
kurals.elementary: When a car starts drifting out of its lane, a warning beeps. This kural says that when your heart starts wanting to be unfair, that is your warning beep: trouble is coming if you don’t steer back.
kurals.university: The couplet is written as an internal monologue: கெடுவல் யான் (“I shall perish”) is what one should say to oneself the moment the heart நடு ஒரீஇ (“having abandoned the middle”) turns toward அல்ல (“what is not [right]”). Commentators differ on emphasis. Varadarasanar and Karunanidhi stress the intention itself as the omen (“if the heart even thinks of it”), while Pope renders it “let man impending ruin’s sign discern.” Either way, injustice is presented as self-destructive, not merely harmful to others. This matches the Manusmriti’s maxim that violated justice destroys the violator, the Qur’anic warning to David that following desire in judgment leads astray, and Plato’s argument that injustice is a disease of the soul.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Justice, being violated, destroys; justice, being preserved, preserves: therefore justice must not be violated, lest violated justice destroy us.”
hinduism.explanation: The Laws of Manu state the principle dharmo rakṣati rakṣitaḥ: dharma (justice) destroys whoever violates it and protects whoever protects it.
hinduism.tie_back: An almost exact counterpart: whoever abandons justice should know it will destroy them.
hinduism.source: Manusmriti 8.15 (trans. G. Bühler, Sacred Books of the East vol. 25)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; Bühler translates dharma as “justice” in this legal context.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.”
christianity.explanation: Paul warns that a person inevitably reaps the consequences of what they sow.
christianity.tie_back: Both warn that wrongdoing carries its own ruin back to the doer.
christianity._accuracy_note: General moral-consequence parallel. It is not specific to departing from impartiality.

islam.quote_or_event: “O David, indeed We have made you a successor upon the earth, so judge between the people in truth and do not follow [your own] desire, as it will lead you astray from the way of Allah.”
islam.explanation: God tells King David to judge by truth and not by personal inclination, warning that following desire leads astray and to punishment.
islam.tie_back: The same inner movement as the Kural: when the heart leaves fairness for desire, ruin follows.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on inner bias as the start of ruin. Addressed to a ruler-judge.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that soweth iniquity shall reap vanity: and the rod of his anger shall fail.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb says whoever sows injustice will harvest emptiness, and his power will fail.
judaism.tie_back: Injustice leads to the doer’s own ruin, the self-warning of the Kural.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on self-inflicted consequence. It lacks the Kural’s introspective “know this yourself” framing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever through desire, hate or fear, Or ignorance should transgress the Dhamma, All his glory fades away Like the moon during the waning half.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names the four biases (agati: desire, hatred, fear, delusion) that lead people to act wrongly, and says whoever is swayed by them declines like the waning moon.
buddhism.tie_back: The agati are exactly the forces that pull a heart away from the “middle.” The Kural and the Sutta both predict decline.
buddhism.source: Sigalovada Sutta, Digha Nikaya 31 (trans. Narada Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close: the four agati are the classical Buddhist list of partialities, and the result is decline.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And there is virgin Justice, the daughter of Zeus, who is honoured and reverenced among the gods who dwell on Olympus, and whenever anyone hurts her with lying slander, she sits beside her father, Zeus the son of Cronos, and tells him of men’s wicked heart, until the people pay for the mad folly …”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod portrays Dike (Justice) as a goddess who reports every injury done to her to Zeus, who then punishes the wrongdoers.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Both warn that turning away from justice brings certain ruin, and Hesiod even locates the problem in the “wicked heart.”
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good match on ruin following injustice. Punishment is external (Zeus) rather than self-recognized.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Then virtue is the health and beauty and well-being of the soul, and vice the disease and weakness and deformity of the same?”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates argues that injustice is to the soul what disease is to the body: it harms the unjust person first.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats departure from justice as self-destruction.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual parallel (injustice harms the agent). Plato’s argument is metaphysical rather than a practical warning.

kurals.tamil:
கெடுவாக வையாது உலகம் நடுவாக
நன்றிக்கண் தங்கியான் தாழ்வு.
kurals.transliteration:
Keduvaaga vaiyaadhu ulagam naduvaaga
Nandrikkan thangiyaan thaazhvu.
kurals.meaning: When a person who stays fair and holds to what is right becomes poor, the world does not regard that as a downfall.
kurals.elementary: If a shopkeeper loses money because she refused to cheat anyone, people don’t think of her as a failure. They respect her even more.
kurals.university: Kural 117 answers an objection that Kural 112 might invite: what if the just person does not prosper? Valluvar grants that the one who நடுவாக நன்றிக்கண் தங்கியான் (“abides in goodness, keeping to the middle”) may suffer தாழ்வு (“lowness, decline, poverty”), but insists the உலகம் will not regard it as கேடு (“ruin”). Here “the world” means the wise or discerning, as Pope (“wise man’s sight”) and Pappaiah (“the great”) make explicit. Social esteem is separated from material fortune: honour tracks justice, not wealth. The theme recurs across traditions: Proverbs’ “better is the poor that walketh in his uprightness,” the Beatitude for those persecuted for righteousness, Socrates’ poverty for the sake of his mission, and the Hindu legend of Harishchandra, who lost everything rather than break his word.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Harishchandra, to honour a promise made to the sage Vishvamitra, gives up his kingdom and wealth and is reduced to selling his wife and son and working at a cremation ground. He never abandons truth, and the gods finally restore and exalt him.
hinduism.explanation: Harishchandra is the classic Indian example of a righteous man whose poverty is a mark of honour rather than disgrace.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s point in story form: the poverty of one who stays righteous is not counted as ruin.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Narrative summary, not a quotation. Harishchandra’s virtue is truthfulness rather than impartiality.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus declares that those who suffer because of their righteousness are blessed, not defeated.
christianity.tie_back: Both reframe hardship caused by righteousness as honour rather than failure.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match. Persecution is broader than poverty.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says true nobility is measured by righteousness, not by tribe or wealth.
islam.tie_back: Both put a person’s standing in their righteousness, not their material state.
islam._accuracy_note: Good parallel on worth measured by righteousness. It does not mention poverty directly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Better is the poor that walketh in his uprightness, than he that is perverse in his ways, though he be rich.”
judaism.explanation: The proverb ranks an upright poor person above a crooked rich one.
judaism.tie_back: Almost exactly the Kural: poverty with uprightness is not degradation.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by matted hair, nor by lineage, nor by birth does one become a holy man. But he in whom truth and righteousness exist — he is pure, he is a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says true worth comes from truth and righteousness, not from outward status.
buddhism.tie_back: Both separate real standing from external circumstances.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Moderate: it addresses birth and outward signs rather than poverty.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Baucis and Philemon, a poor old couple in Phrygia, are the only household to welcome the disguised gods Jupiter and Mercury. The gods spare them when the region is flooded, turn their hut into a temple, and grant their wish to serve it and to die together.
greek_mythology.explanation: The myth honours a poor but righteous couple above their wealthier, inhospitable neighbours.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Their poverty is no mark of lowness in the gods’ eyes; their goodness is what counts.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Summary, not a quotation. The virtue is piety and hospitality rather than impartiality. A Roman telling of a Greek-world myth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “my occupation quite absorbs me, and I have no time to give either to any public matter of interest or to any concern of my own, but I am in utter poverty by reason of my devotion to the god.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates tells the jury that his poverty is the direct result of his commitment to his philosophical mission.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates is a model of poverty that comes from integrity, and history has honoured rather than despised it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good parallel of poverty resulting from principled living. His principle is truth-seeking rather than impartiality.

kurals.tamil:
சமன்செய்து சீர்தூக்குங் கோல்போல் அமைந்தொருபால்
கோடாமை சான்றோர்க் கணி.
kurals.transliteration:
Saman seydhu seerthookkung kolpol amaindhorupaal
Kodaamai saandrork kani.
kurals.meaning: Like a balance-beam that first sets itself level and then weighs things exactly, the noble person stays steady and does not lean to either side; this is their true ornament.
kurals.elementary: A good weighing scale sits perfectly flat before you put anything on it, then shows the true weight, no matter whose apples they are. A fair person is like that scale: steady and not tipping toward anyone.
kurals.university: This is the chapter’s central image. The துலாக்கோல் (tulaakkol, balance-beam) first சமன்செய்து (“makes itself even”), then சீர்தூக்கும் (“weighs rightly”), and does not ஒருபால் கோடாமை (“incline to one side”). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah stress the two-stage sequence: the judge must first be internally level, free of prior bias, and only then evaluate. That is a sharp account of impartiality as a disposition as well as a procedure. The scale is a near-universal emblem of justice: Zeus’s golden scales in Homer, the Qur’anic mīzān, the “just balances” of Leviticus, and the Dhammapada’s sage who weighs good and evil “as if holding a balance-scale.” Aristotle’s description of the judge as “animate justice” and “intermediate” states the same idea philosophically. The second line repeats the refrain of Kural 115, linking inner steadiness under fortune to outer impartiality in judgment.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Shibi, when a hawk demands a dove that has taken refuge with him, refuses to wrong either bird. He offers his own flesh equal in weight to the dove, placing it on a scale, and finally climbs onto the scale himself, after which the gods (Indra and Agni in disguise) reveal themselves and praise him.
hinduism.explanation: In the Mahabharata, Shibi will not favour the dove at the hawk’s expense or the hawk at the dove’s, and a literal pair of scales settles the matter.
hinduism.tie_back: An Indian story in which the scale itself is the emblem of refusing to lean toward either party.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Shibi and the dove)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Narrative summary, not a quotation. The story centres on self-sacrifice and protection; impartiality between the two claimants is a secondary element.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his critics to judge by what is truly right, not by surface impressions.
christianity.tie_back: Like the level scale, righteous judgment weighs the real substance and not appearances or bias.
christianity._accuracy_note: Parallel on unbiased judgment. It has no balance imagery.

islam.quote_or_event: “That you not transgress within the balance. And establish weight in justice and do not make deficient the balance.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says God set up the cosmic balance (al-mīzān) and commands people not to violate it but to weigh with justice.
islam.tie_back: The same image of the balance as the model of justice, which must not be tipped.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close: the balance is both literal and a symbol of cosmic justice.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment, in meteyard, in weight, or in measure. Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have”
judaism.explanation: The Torah puts judgment and weights and measures in the same command: both must be exact and fair.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s scale-and-judgment pairing appears here in one sentence.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the scale and justice link. The Torah verse is more literal and commercial.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by observing silence does one become a sage, if he be foolish and ignorant. But that man is wise who, as if holding a balance-scale accepts only the good.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada uses a balance-scale image: the true sage weighs things carefully, taking the good and rejecting the evil.
buddhism.tie_back: A direct balance-scale metaphor for the discerning person, as in the Kural.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Same image. The Dhammapada uses it for moral discernment rather than impartiality between persons.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “the father of all balanced his golden scales and placed a doom in each of them, one for Achilles and the other for Hector. As he held the scales by the middle, the doom of Hector fell down deep into the house of Hades”
greek_mythology.explanation: Even Zeus, who pities Hector, does not decide by favour; he weighs the two fates on his golden scales, holding them “by the middle,” and accepts the result.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The balance held level at the centre, deciding without favour, is the Kural’s image.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong image match, including holding the scale by the middle. What is weighed is fate rather than a legal case.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “to go to the judge is to go to justice; for the nature of the judge is to be a sort of animate justice; and they seek the judge as an intermediate”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle describes the judge as justice in living form: a mean point that restores equality between two parties.
philosophy.tie_back: Aristotle’s judge-as-intermediate is the philosophical version of the Kural’s level balance-beam.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics V.4 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close conceptually (the judge as the balanced middle). Aristotle uses the image of a divided line rather than scales.

kurals.tamil:
சொற்கோட்டம் இல்லது செப்பம் ஒருதலையா
உட்கோட்டம் இன்மை பெறின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Sorkottam illadhu seppam orudhalaiyaa
Utkottam inmai perin.
kurals.meaning: Speech free of crookedness counts as true fairness only when the heart itself is firmly free of any crookedness or bias.
kurals.elementary: A shiny apple can still be rotten inside. Saying fair-sounding words isn’t enough; your heart has to be fair on the inside too, and then your words will be truly straight.
kurals.university: The couplet pairs சொற்கோட்டம் (“crookedness of word”) with உட்கோட்டம் (“inner crookedness”) and makes the first depend on the second: straight speech is செப்பம் (rectitude) only if one ஒருதலையா (“definitely, without fail”) has an unbent inner state. The target is the sophisticated partiality of someone who says the right things while privately favouring one side. That concern fits a chapter aimed at those who arbitrate, give testimony or advise. Commentators read it both ways. Varadarasanar treats inner straightness as the condition, while Pappaiah and Karunanidhi treat straight speech as its natural result. The same principle, that honest speech flows from an honest heart, appears in Jesus’ “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh,” Achilles’ contempt for the man “who says one thing while he hides another in his heart,” and Plato’s distinction between the lie in words and the “true lie” in the soul.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Austerity of speech consists in speaking words that are truthful, pleasing, beneficial, and not agitating to others, and also in regularly reciting Vedic literature.”
hinduism.explanation: The Gita treats right speech as a discipline (tapas) grouped with discipline of mind and body in the neighbouring verses.
hinduism.tie_back: Both treat truthful, straight speech as a moral discipline linked to inner purity.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Moderate. The Gita describes good speech but does not make it depend on inner impartiality.

christianity.quote_or_event: “for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that words reveal and flow from what fills the heart.
christianity.tie_back: The same dependence the Kural states: straight words need a straight heart.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close on the heart-to-speech link. It is not specific to fairness.

islam.quote_or_event: “So follow not [personal] inclination, lest you not be just. And if you distort [your testimony] or refuse [to give it], then indeed Allah is ever, with what you do, Acquainted.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an links inner inclination (hawā) with distorted testimony, and warns that God sees both.
islam.tie_back: Inner bias and twisted words are named together, the Kural’s utkottam and sorkottam.
islam._accuracy_note: Excellent match on inner bias producing distorted speech in a justice context.

judaism.quote_or_event: “He that walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm describes the person fit to dwell with God as one whose truthfulness goes all the way into the heart.
judaism.tie_back: “Speaketh the truth in his heart” is close to the Kural’s requirement that straightness be internal as well as spoken.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Mind precedes all mental states. Mind is their chief; they are all mind-wrought. If with a pure mind a person speaks or acts happiness follows him like his never-departing shadow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada opens by teaching that the mind comes first and speech and action follow from it.
buddhism.tie_back: Both locate the source of straight speech in the state of the mind.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on mind preceding speech. It does not mention fairness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Him do I hate even as the gates of hell who says one thing while he hides another in his heart; therefore I will say what I mean.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles rejects Agamemnon’s envoys, declaring that he despises anyone whose words differ from their heart.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The gap between heart and speech that the Kural condemns, named in Homer.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close on heart-speech consistency. Achilles speaks of candour rather than impartiality.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “the true lie, if such an expression may be allowed, is hated of gods and men” … “the lie in words is only a kind of imitation and shadowy image of a previous affection of the soul”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates distinguishes the lie in words from the “true lie” in the soul, and says spoken falsehood is only a shadow of a prior distortion inside.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural has the same two layers: crookedness in word depends on crookedness within.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel. Plato’s concern is false belief rather than bias.

kurals.tamil:
வாணிகம் செய்வார்க்கு வாணிகம் பேணிப்
பிறவும் தமபோல் செயின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vaanigam seyvaarkku vaanigam penip
Piravum thamapol seyin.
kurals.meaning: For those who trade, the true way of trade is to guard and deal with other people’s goods and interests as carefully as their own.
kurals.elementary: A good shopkeeper weighs your rice as carefully as if it were for her own family, and charges you the same fair price she’d want to pay herself. That’s what honest business means.
kurals.university: The chapter closes by applying impartiality to commerce, the everyday setting where people most often weigh and measure for one another. பிறவும் தமபோல் (“others’ [goods] as their own”) is the principle: the merchant must take no more and give no less than they would accept if the roles were reversed. Parimelazhagar notes the scale imagery carried over from Kural 118, since trade literally involves weighing. The doubled வாணிகம் (“trade … trade”) is emphatic: only this is real trade, and anything else is disguised theft. Parallels include the Qur’anic curse on those who give short measure, the Talmudic tradition that the first question at the heavenly judgment is “Did you conduct business faithfully?”, Hesiod’s counsel to give fair measure “or better,” and Kant’s honest shopkeeper who charges a child the same as anyone else. Kant adds that honesty practised only because it pays is not yet fully moral, which fits the Kural’s demand for inner straightness in Kural 119.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “He is a perfect yogī who, by comparison to his own self, sees the true equality of all beings, in both their happiness and their distress, O Arjuna!”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna praises the person who judges others’ joys and sufferings by comparison with their own (ātmaupamya).
hinduism.tie_back: The same “as one’s own” standard the Kural applies to a merchant’s dealings.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the “others as oneself” principle. The Gita says nothing about trade.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus gives the Golden Rule as the summary of the whole law.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural applies the Golden Rule to buying and selling.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong principle match. It is not specific to commerce.

islam.quote_or_event: “Woe to those who give less [than due], Who, when they take a measure from people, take in full. But if they give by measure or by weight to them, they cause loss.”
islam.explanation: Surah al-Mutaffifin (“The Defrauders”) condemns traders who demand full measure for themselves but short others.
islam.tie_back: The exact opposite of the Kural’s ideal: these traders use a double standard, one for themselves and another for others.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one, stated as a negative example in a commercial context.

judaism.quote_or_event: “when a person is brought to judgment for the life he lived in this world, they say to him in the order of that verse: Did you conduct business faithfully?”
judaism.explanation: Rava teaches that the very first question asked at the heavenly judgment is whether one did business honestly (nasata ve-natata be-emunah).
judaism.tie_back: Both make honest trade a central religious and moral test.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the moral weight of honest business. It does not state the “as one’s own” formula.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “All tremble at violence; life is dear to all. Putting oneself in the place of another, one should not kill nor cause another to kill.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada grounds ethics in putting oneself in another’s place.
buddhism.tie_back: The same self-other comparison underlies the Kural’s rule of treating others’ goods as one’s own.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shares the empathy principle. It is about non-violence, not commerce.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Take fair measure from your neighbour and pay him back fairly with the same measure, or better, if you can; so that if you are in need afterwards, you may find him sure.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod advises his brother to deal with neighbours using an honest measure, returning as much or more.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The same measure for self and other is the Kural’s formula for honest trade.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very close on fair measure. Hesiod’s motive is partly prudential (future help).

philosophy.quote_or_event: “it is always a matter of duty that a dealer should not over charge an inexperienced purchaser; and wherever there is much commerce the prudent tradesman does not overcharge, but keeps a fixed price for everyone, so that a child buys of him as well as any other.”
philosophy.explanation: Kant’s famous shopkeeper charges everyone, even a child, the same fair price. Kant adds that doing so only out of self-interest would not yet show true moral worth.
philosophy.tie_back: The honest merchant who treats every buyer alike is the Kural’s ideal. Kant’s caveat about motive echoes Kural 119’s demand for an unbent heart.
philosophy.source: Immanuel Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals, First Section (trans. T. K. Abbott)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match on impartial, honest trade. Kant uses the example to separate duty from prudence.
